entries.meaning: Bowing his head at the sage's lotus feet, Rāma—the lord of gods, people and sages—set out into the forest. Rāma went ahead, his younger brother followed behind, both dressed closely in excellent ascetic garb, while Śrī Sītā shone between them as māyā stands between Brahman and the individual soul. Rivers, forests, mountains and difficult passes recognized their Lord and gave them an excellent path; wherever divine Rāma went, clouds made shade in the sky. On the road he met the demon Virādha and struck him down as soon as he advanced. Virādha at once regained his beautiful form, and Rāma, seeing him afflicted, sent him to his own abode. Then the Lord came to the place where sage Śarabhaṅga dwelt, accompanied by beautiful Lakṣmaṇa and Jānakī. The eminent sage drank respectfully and without cease, like bees with his eyes, the lotus of Rāma's face, and blessed indeed was Śarabhaṅga's birth.

Śarabhaṅga said, ‘Hear me, compassionate hero of Raghu, royal swan of Śiva's mind-lake. I was setting out for Brahmā's abode when I heard that Rāma would come into the forest. I watched the road day and night; now, seeing you, Lord, my heart is soothed. I lack every spiritual discipline, but knowing your servant to be helpless you showed grace. God, you owe me nothing: you have upheld your own vow, O stealer of your servant's heart. Remain for the sake of the helpless until, relinquishing this body, I meet you.’ Śarabhaṅga offered to the Lord all the yoga, sacrifice, recitation, austerity and vows he had performed and received devotion as his boon. He then prepared a funeral pyre, sat down with every attachment released from his heart, and prayed: ‘May Śrī Rāma—dark-bodied like a blue cloud and accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa—dwell forever in my heart in manifest form.’

Having spoken thus, Śarabhaṅga burned his body in yogic fire and, by Rāma's grace, departed for Vaikuṇṭha. He did not therefore become dissolved into Hari, for from the outset he had chosen discriminating devotion as his boon. Seeing the eminent sage's destiny, the assembled seers became especially happy in their hearts and all the hosts of sages praised Rāma: ‘Victory to the source of compassion, benefactor of those who surrender!’ Rāma then moved deeper into the forest, with many eminent sages following. Seeing a mass of bones, Rāma was filled with compassion and asked the sages about it. They replied, ‘Why ask though you know, Master? You see all and know every heart. Hordes of demons have eaten all the sages.’ Hearing this, Rāma's eyes filled with tears. Raising his arm, he vowed to rid the earth of demons, and went from hermitage to hermitage bringing happiness to all the sages.

Sutīkṣṇa, the wise disciple of sage Agastya, loved the Lord and served Rāma's feet in mind, action and speech; even in dream he trusted no other god. Hearing with his own ears that the Lord was coming, he ran eagerly while imagining the meeting: ‘O Fate, will Rāma, friend of the helpless, show mercy to a rogue like me? Will Lord Rāma meet me with Lakṣmaṇa as one meets his own servant? My heart has no firm confidence: it contains neither devotion, detachment nor knowledge; I have no holy company, yoga, recitation, vigil, or firm love for his lotus feet. Yet the treasury of compassion has one rule: one who has no other refuge is dear to him. Today my eyes will bear fruit by seeing the lotus face that frees one from becoming.’ The sage was immersed in overwhelming love; he could not tell direction from quarter, path or destination, sometimes turned back, and sometimes danced while singing Rāma's virtues. Having obtained unbroken loving devotion, he failed to see the Lord, who watched hidden behind a tree. Seeing his intense love, Rāma appeared within his heart and removed the fear of becoming. The sage sat motionless in the road, his thrilled body like a jackfruit. Rāma came near, delighted by his servant's state, and tried repeatedly to awaken him; absorbed in the joy born of meditation, he did not wake. Rāma then concealed his royal form and revealed his four-armed form in the sage's heart. Agitated, the sage awoke like a fine serpent deprived of its jewel and saw before him dark-bodied Rāma, abode of bliss, with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa. He fell like a staff and clasped the Lord's feet; immersed in love, the greatly blessed sage was raised and held to Rāma's broad breast. Their meeting looked like a tamāla tree embracing a golden tree. The sage stood gazing at Rāma's face as motionless as a figure drawn in a picture, then gradually recovered composure, clasped his feet again and again, brought the Lord to his hermitage, and worshipped him in many ways.

The sage said, ‘Lord, hear my prayer: how can I praise you? Your greatness is boundless and my understanding slight; a firefly's light before the sun is mine before you. I continually bow to the hero of Raghu: his body is dark as a garland of blue lotuses, matted locks crown him, ascetic bark clothes him, and he holds bow and arrow with a quiver at his waist. He is consuming fire for delusion's dense forest and the sun for the lotus-grove of saints; lion to the elephant-herd of demons, may he always protect us; hawk to the bird of worldly becoming, may he save us. His reddish eyes and lovely form are red lotuses; he is the moon for the cakora birds of Sītā's eyes, a young swan in Śiva's heart-lake. I bow to Rāma, broad of chest and arm. Garuḍa who devours the serpent of doubt, he quiets the harsh poison of futile argument. Destroyer of becoming, delight of the gods' assembly, may that shelter of grace always protect us. Form both attributeless and attributed, unequal and equal, incomparable and beyond knowledge, speech and senses; spotless, whole, faultless and boundless—I bow to Rāma, who relieves the earth's burden. A pleasure-garden of wish-fulfilling trees for devotees, he terrifies anger, greed, pride and desire; consummately gracious, a bridge across becoming's ocean, banner of the solar race, may he always protect us. Abode of incomparable strength, majesty and power, his Name wholly destroys Kali's immense impurity. Armour of dharma, giver of joy, treasury of virtues—may Rāma always extend blessedness to me. Though passionless, all-pervading and imperishable, forever dwelling in every heart, let the enemy of Khara nevertheless dwell in the forest of my mind with Lakṣmaṇa and Śrī Sītā. Those who know may know you as both with and without attributes, Master, knower within every heart; but may lotus-eyed Rāma, lord of Kosala, make my heart his home. Never let this conviction leave me: I am the servant and Rāma is my master.’ Pleased, Rāma embraced him and offered whatever boon he wished. The sage confessed he had never asked a boon and could not judge true from false, asking Rāma to give whatever seemed best. Rāma granted unbroken devotion, detachment, discernment, and every virtue and knowledge. The sage accepted, then asked for the boon dear to him: that bow-and-arrow-bearing Rāma, with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, dwell desirelessly and forever like a moon in the sky of his heart.

words: to Śrī Rāma, hero of Raghu

entries.meaning: Saying ‘So be it,’ the abode of Lakṣmī joyfully set out toward the sage Agastya. Sutīkṣṇa explained that many days had passed since he had seen his teacher because he had come to this hermitage; now he wished to accompany the Lord to his teacher, though Rāma owed him no favour. Seeing the sage's clever devotion, the treasury of compassion took him along while the two brothers smiled. As Sutīkṣṇa described his incomparable devotion on the road, the lord of the gods reached the sage's hermitage. Sutīkṣṇa at once went to his teacher, prostrated, and announced, ‘Lord, the princes of the lord of Kosala have come to meet you—the supports of the world: Rāma with Lakṣmaṇa and Vaidehī, whom you contemplate night and day.’ Hearing this, Agastya immediately ran forth; on seeing Hari his eyes filled with tears. Both brothers fell at the sage's lotus feet, and the seer lovingly raised them and held them to his heart. The wise sage respectfully asked after their welfare, brought excellent seats, seated them, and worshipped the Lord in many ways, declaring none as fortunate as himself. All the other gathered sages rejoiced to behold the source of happiness. Seated amid the assembly of sages and facing them all, Rāma's body was like the autumn moon watched by a host of cakora birds.
